Both can be evaluated at a cost linear in the numbers of products and periods. Our method estimates demand for 2,000 products from 2,000 selling periods in under ten minutes.
item.dc:creator: Chenhao Wang, Hansheng Jiang, Ningyuan Chen

item.title: Sparse Sum-of-Squares Layers for Certified Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.34590v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A central limitation of modern machine learning systems is the lack of formal certificates guaranteeing their behavior beyond empirical, sample-based evaluation. Sum-of-squares (SOS) methods provide such guarantees by certifying polynomial inequalities over continuous domains via semidefinite programming (SDP). While prior work has introduced SDP layers as differentiable components in neural networks, repeated learning calls can lose the computational benefit of the forward program's sparse representation. We propose Sparse SOS Layers, differentiable value layers whose backward passes reuse the local coordinates of the forward solve. Under a fixed template and learned objective coefficients, each layer avoids building dense certificates and reuses its sparse structure across training steps. Compared with existing methods, our approach achieves up to 2.7 times speedup in total warm-call time, with nearly 100 times lower memory usage (1.7 vs. 160 GiB) for relatively large problem sizes for the tested dense parameterization. Experiments cover sparse polynomial certification, pendulum control, combinatorial relaxations, robotics projection, oscillator chains, and pose graph synchronization. A design study achieves zero certified violations across unseen problem instances and sizes, while requiring roughly 7 times fewer optimization solves than estimating gradients by perturbing the objective coefficients and re-solving the problem (finite differences). These results show that sparse certificate values can be effectively integrated into learning pipelines when the backward pass respects the verifier's structure.
item.dc:creator: Ege Gursoy, Nicolas Mansard

item.title: A Discontinuous Galerkin Method for Biharmonic Dirichlet Control Problems With Patch Reconstruction
item.description: arXiv:2610.34669v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we present and analyze an interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin method for Dirichlet boundary control problems governed by the biharmonic equation, with the control imposed through the normal derivative. The method is based on a reconstructed discontinuous approximation that admits an arbitrarily high-order approximation space with only one unknown per element. We construct a discretization that approximates the state and adjoint state in this space and derive a priori error estimates in the energy and $L^2$ norms. The analysis is carried out under the limited regularity available on polygonal domains by means of a medius argument. Numerical experiments are provided to support the predicted convergence rates.
item.dc:creator: Wei Gong, Ruo Li, Jun Yin

item.title: Rank-one Factored Gradient Descent without Restricted Isometry: Application to Quantum Pure State Tomography on Multi-Qubits
item.description: arXiv:2610.34696v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Factored gradient descent (FGD) is a scalable nonconvex method for low-rank positive semidefinite matrix recovery, in which the rank and positivity constraints are satisfied automatically by the factorization. Most of the existing theory that certifies benignity of its loss landscape, however, relies on a restricted isometry property (RIP) of the measurement map. In quantum state tomography, one of its applications, the measurements that can be acquired with stable statistics are limited by detection efficiency and drift to Pauli observables of low weight; we first show that under such partial-weight Pauli measurements RIP fails in the worst possible way. We then bundle the mutually commuting observables setting by setting, pushing the state forward to the probability distribution of each setting, and introduce a max-sliced total-variation loss. On the stratum where the setting attaining the maximum is unique there is no spurious local minimum, and provided only that the measurement map is injective on generic pure states, the global minimum is the truth up to a phase. Finally we verify these claims numerically on four qubits and compare against FGD with the ordinary loss.
item.dc:creator: Takahiro Kajisa

item.title: Follow the Regularized Leader Does Not Converge in Constrained Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.35004v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Follow the regularized leader (FTRL) is a foundational algorithm in online learning whose regret properties have been extensively studied for decades. However, in stark contrast to mirror descent---and gradient descent in particular---the convergence of FTRL to first-order stationary points in constrained nonconvex optimization was not well understood. In this paper, we show that continuous-time FTRL can fail to converge even asymptotically in infinitely smooth constrained optimization problems: its Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) gap can remain bounded away from zero indefinitely. This is especially surprising in light of the fact that continuous-time FTRL guarantees a monotonic improvement of the objective value. As a result, we establish that non-convergent behavior of no-regret dynamics---which besets general variational inequality problems---can occur even in potential systems. From a technical standpoint, our construction relies on an infinitely differentiable function where the gradient flow dynamics exhibit decelerating oscillations without ever converging pointwise, which we in turn embed into higher-dimensional FTRL dynamics that sustain a perpetually large KKT gap. We complement our negative result by showing that FTRL with Euclidean regularization does converge when the objective function is analytic. This shows that the analytic property plays a more fundamental role for FTRL than for gradient flow: it governs not only pointwise convergence, but convergence to first-order stationarity itself.
item.dc:creator: Ioannis Anagnostides, Ioannis Panageas, Nikolas Patris, Tuomas Sandholm

item.title: Adaptive Control for General Nonlinear Stochastic Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.35182v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper extends the least-squares and certainty-equivalence minimum-variance framework of classical linear self-tuning regulators to a broad class of nonlinearly parameterized systems with compact parameter spaces, including commonly used deep neural network models. First, historical nonlinear least-squares fitting guarantees are converted into online one-step prediction bounds under a general modulus of continuity, with explicit regret rates under parameter Lipschitz continuity and finite-moment noise. Second, approximate NLS estimation combined with certainty-equivalence control achieves closed-loop stability and asymptotically optimal tracking under mild conditions without requiring excitation or parameter identifiability. Explicit closed-loop regret and tracking error rates are established in the parameter-Lipschitz case, and closed-loop examples show that the regret rates cannot, in general, be improved for this regulator. Finally, robustness to small unmodeled dynamics is established by showing that closed-loop stability is preserved and the tracking error bounds comprise a vanishing term and a residual term determined by the model discrepancy.
item.dc:creator: Haizheng Li

item.title: Understanding Practical Optimization in Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.35209v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern machine learning relies on practical optimization methods that often differ from the algorithms studied in classical analyses: they train submodels, clip or normalize gradients, use layer-wise non-Euclidean directions, or approximate costly inner computations. This thesis analyzes the objective, assumptions, update, and computation defined by these procedures, rather than those of simplified proxies. For submodel training, we show that Independent Subnetwork Training can converge to a shifted fixed point because sketching before differentiation biases the update for the original objective. Model-Agnostic Sparsified Training instead incorporates the sketch distribution into its objective, which makes sketched gradients unbiased and admits convergence guarantees. For private optimization, we show that adaptive quantile clipping retains bias at any fixed quantile, while suitable quantile schedules recover near-optimal nonconvex rates under heavy-tailed noise. We then combine smoothed normalization with error compensation and obtain distributed private convergence guarantees under standard assumptions, without assuming bounded gradients. For optimizers based on linear minimization oracles, we develop and validate a layer-wise generalized smoothness model and build on it the Gluon framework for Muon- and Scion-style methods. We also show that the approximate orthogonalization in Muon matters: less precise orthogonalization calls for smaller stepsizes, so its precision should be tuned together with the learning rate. Overall, practical methods are better understood when theory retains the features that determine their optimization behavior.
item.dc:creator: Egor Shulgin

item.title: Regularization and Full Support for the CBO Equation with Measure Initial Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.35266v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove global well-posedness and regularization for the isotropic consensus-based optimization equation with initial probability measures of finite fourth moment. Under suitable weight decay assumptions, after any nonconstant consensus motion, both the density and the consensus trajectory become smooth, and all spatial Sobolev norms are locally bounded in time. The proof uses a Fourier commutator estimate, localization and iteration, followed by a nonlinear time bootstrap. Counterexamples show that smoothing can fail at a stationary consensus point. For non-Dirac initial data, we also prove positivity away from the consensus point and full support at every positive time in all dimensions.
item.dc:creator: Lukang Sun

item.title: Accelerated Push-Pull with Local Updates for Decentralized Stochastic Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.35275v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider decentralized stochastic nonconvex optimization over directed networks. Push--Pull provides an efficient decentralized optimization framework for such networks, but in the stochastic setting, gradient variance can slow its convergence and complicate the analysis of linear speedup. Motivated by this observation, we incorporate recursive momentum into stochastic Push--Pull for variance reduction, yielding the accelerated stochastic Push--Pull (ASPP) algorithm. Under mean-squared smoothness, we prove that ASPP improves the convergence rate of stochastic Push--Pull and achieves asymptotic linear speedup with respect to the number of agents. To further reduce communication, we develop LASPP, a local-update variant of ASPP that allows each agent to perform multiple local updates between communication rounds. We show that LASPP achieves an additional asymptotic linear speedup with respect to the number of local steps. With a suitable number of local steps, LASPP reduces communication complexity while maintaining the same stochastic gradient complexity as ASPP. Numerical experiments on real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Sheng Dong, Weiguo Xia, Huijie Tao

item.title: Initialization Stability and Convergence of Projected Langevin Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.35369v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The entropic regularized optimal transport (EOT) plays a fundamental role in the computation of optimal transport. In \cite{CLP}, the authors proposed a gradient flow approach to EOT, and derived a projected Langevin diffusion that converges in distribution to the solution of EOT when initialized with a coupling between the two given marginals. In this paper, motivated by samplings of optimal couplings for EOT, we analyze the projected Langevin dynamics with arbitrary initial distribution, and prove that its long time behavior is the same as if it was initialized from a coupling.
item.dc:creator: Qi Feng, Nathan Sauldubois, Xin Zhang

item.title: Benchmarking quantum-annealing-based approaches for factory layout planning
item.description: arXiv:2610.35478v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The earlystage of factory layout planning has a direct effect on the operating costs, efficiency, and productivity of manufacturing systems. Conventional automated planning approaches often face a trade-off between solution quality and computational effort. Recent studies have investigated the potential of quantum annealing (QA) for solving factory layout planning problems. However, existing studies have mainly focused on individual QA-based formulations, whereas current hybrid QA solvers support multiple model types that combine QA and classical methods. To explore the potential of QA for factory layout planning, this paper benchmarks four QA based approaches implemented with the corresponding solvers, including an iterative binary quadratic model (IBQM), a hybrid discrete quadratic model (HDQM), a hybrid constrained quadratic model (HCQM), and a hybrid nonlinear model (HNLM). To improve scalability, an iterative decomposition strategy is developed for IBQM, while a candidate selection procedure is introduced for HDQM. The approaches are benchmarked against genetic algorithm, particle swarm optimization, and a hybrid tabu search and simulated annealing approach on 14 layout instances with different layout sizes, geometric complexity, spatial restrictions, and transport route configurations. The comparative analysis considers solution quality, computation time, and scalability. The results show that QA-based approaches achieve competitive solution quality and substantial computational advantages, reducing computation time by up to 94.51% relative to the classical reference methods. Among them, IBQM obtains the best solution quality in 78.6% of the instances, with a maximum improvement of 17.41% associated with an 81.34% reduction in computation time. These findings provide a basis for their further application in industrial layout planning.
item.dc:creator: Xiangqian Wu, Philipp Schworm, Marcel Wagner, Jan C. Aurich

item.title: SCAFFOLD under Hessian Similarity: Sharp Convergence Rates
item.description: arXiv:2610.35663v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: One of the main challenges of federated learning is heterogeneous data split among the clients, leading to biased local updates called client drift. The SCAFFOLD algorithm (Karimireddy et al., 2020) corrects client drift with control variates, but its relation to the similarity of client data is not yet fully understood: the original similarity-based guarantees cover only quadratics with a stronger second-order similarity assumption, and a follow-up weakly convex analysis (Luo et al., 2025) obtains a $\sqrt{L\delta}$ dependence for $L$-smooth losses with averaged Hessian similarity $\delta$. We analyze SCAFFOLD with minibatch-based control variates and establish linear dependence on Hessian similarity beyond quadratics, for both convex and nonconvex objectives. In particular, for convex objectives with exact gradients, $R$ SCAFFOLD rounds with $K$ local steps lead to an objective gap of order $(L/K+\delta)D_0^2/R$, where $D_0$ is the initial distance to a minimizer. When $K=\Theta(L/\delta)$, it improves the minibatch SGD rate by a factor $\Theta(L/\delta)$. For nonconvex objectives, we prove an analogous stationarity guarantee under uniform Hessian similarity for a client-selection variant. In both settings, we extend these guarantees to stochastic gradients and prove matching lower bounds for the analyzed methods with constant local stepsizes. We also show that, under partial participation, even identical clients need not obtain the full communication benefit of additional local steps.
item.dc:creator: Zhirayr Tovmasyan, Slavom\'ir Hanzely, Egor Shulgin, Peter Richt\'arik, Sebastian U. Stich

item.title: Computing Data-Aware Diagonal Frame Decompositions
item.description: arXiv:2610.35691v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a method for computing a specific type of matrix decomposition that combines a structured framework with data-driven adaptation. This framework allows for an efficient and stable representation of signals or images using frames by identifying sets of vectors that naturally capture the essential features of the given data. The resulting decomposition enables the development of regularization techniques that enhance the quality of reconstruction by preserving important signal characteristics while suppressing noise. We develop an optimization-based algorithm to compute the decomposition and establish convergence properties of the resulting iterates. Numerical experiments on synthetic data and tomographic image reconstruction illustrate the behavior of the proposed method and its performance compared to conventional spectral regularization methods.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Ebner, Dirk Lorenz, Mathias Staudigl

item.title: Optimal tradeoffs between variance and sensitivity, via Hellinger-Kantorovich geometry
item.description: arXiv:2610.35858v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While the goal of classical statistical theory is to minimize the variance of unbiased estimators, an additional goal of some recent research is to minimize or constrain other notions of the instability of estimators. In particular, a subset of the authors recently introduced a notion of instability termed "sensitivity", which represents the expected amount that an estimator would change if its inputs were infinitesimally perturbed. In this work, we study the multiobjective problem of minimizing both the variance and sensitivity over unbiased estimators in a given statistical model, and we aim to determine Pareto optimal tradeoffs between these two objectives. Our main results show that the Pareto front for these tradeoffs is precisely determined by endowing the statistical model with the Hellinger-Kantorovich geometry, which interpolates between the Hellinger and Wasserstein geometries that are known to be associated, respectively, with the separate minimization of variance and sensitivity. We also develop a $Z$-estimation technique which constructs estimators that asymptotically achieve Pareto optimal pairs of variance and sensitivity. While computing the Pareto front and constructing the resulting estimators in practice requires solving a continuum of partial differential equations, we fully execute this program in some parametric examples of interest where the analysis is already non-trivial. Our results also shed light on some classical statistical problems, for example by showing that the maximum likelihood estimator achieves the smallest asymptotic sensitivity among all estimators achieving the optimal asymptotic variance.
item.dc:creator: Adam Quinn Jaffe, Congwei Yang, Nicol\'as Garc\'ia Trillos, Bodhisattva Sen

item.title: Dimension in Polynomial Variational Inequalities
item.description: arXiv:2001.09435v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the dimension of the solution set of a variational inequality whose operator is polynomial and whose constraint set is defined by finitely many convex polynomial inequalities and affine equations. Under the Abadie constraint qualification, we bound this dimension from above in terms of the ranks of the Jacobian matrices of the associated Karush--Kuhn--Tucker maps; the bound is attained in nontrivial examples and yields a sufficient condition for finiteness of the solution set. For polynomial complementarity problems, the bound is expressed through principal submatrices of the Jacobian matrix of the operator, and the resulting finiteness criterion extends the classical nondegeneracy condition for linear complementarity problems.
item.dc:creator: Vu Trung Hieu

item.title: Analytical benchmark problems and methodological framework for the assessment and comparison of multifidelity optimization methods
item.description: arXiv:2204.07867v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper introduces a comprehensive benchmarking framework that includes: (i) a suite of analytical benchmark optimization problems designed to stress-test and validate multifidelity methods; (ii) a set of assessment metrics for quantifying and comparing performance over measurable objectives; and (iii) the classification, evaluation, and comparison of several families of multifidelity optimization methods and frameworks using the proposed benchmarks to identify their respective strengths and weaknesses in real-world scenarios. The proposed benchmark problems are analytically defined functions carefully selected to capture mathematical challenges commonly encountered in real-world applications, including high dimensionality, multimodality, discontinuities, and noise. Their closed-form nature ensures computational efficiency, high reproducibility, and a clear separation of algorithmic behavior from numerical artifacts. The accompanying performance metrics support the systematic evaluation of multifidelity methods, measuring both optimization effectiveness and global approximation accuracy. By providing a rigorous, reproducible, and accessible benchmarking framework, this work aims to enable the broader community to understand, compare, and advance multifidelity optimization methods for complex problems in science and engineering.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Mainini, L., Serani, A., Pehlivan-Solak, H. et al. Analytical benchmark problems and methodological framework for the assessment and comparison of multifidelity optimization methods. Arch Computat Methods Eng 33, 2969-3000 (2026)
item.dc:creator: L. Mainini, A. Serani, H. Pehlivan, F. Di Fiore, M. P. Rumpfkeil, E. Minisci, D. Quagliarella, S. Yildiz, S. Ficini, R. Pellegrini, A. Thelen, D. Bryson, M. Nikbay, M. Diez, P. Beran

item.title: Optimal control problems governed by time-fractional diffusion equations with control constraint
item.description: arXiv:2210.16818v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A class of optimal control problems governed by linear fractional diffusion equation with control constraint is considered. We first establish some results on the existence of strong solution to the state equation and the existence of optimal solutions for the optimal control problem. Then we derive first-and second-order optimality conditions for locally optimal solutions to the problem.
item.dc:creator: Bui Trong Kien, Bui Ngoc Muoi, Ching-Feng Wen, Jen-Chih Yao

item.title: Mini-Batch Stochastic Conjugate Gradient Algorithms with Minimal Variance
item.description: arXiv:2306.00459v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) methods have gained widespread popularity for solving large-scale optimization problems. However, the inherent variance in SGD often leads to slow convergence rates. We introduce a family of unbiased stochastic gradient estimators that encompasses existing estimators from the literature and identify a gradient estimator that not only maintains unbiasedness but also achieves minimal variance. Compared with the existing estimator used in SGD algorithms, the proposed estimator demonstrates a significant reduction in variance. By utilizing this stochastic gradient estimator to approximate the full gradient, we propose two mini-batch stochastic conjugate gradient algorithms with minimal variance. Under the assumptions of strong convexity and smoothness on the objective function, we prove that the two algorithms achieve linear convergence rates. Numerical experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed gradient estimator in reducing variance and demonstrate that the two stochastic conjugate gradient algorithms exhibit accelerated convergence rates and enhanced stability.
item.dc:creator: Caixia Kou, Feifei Gao, Yu-Hong Dai

item.title: Globally Optimal Solutions to a Class of Fractional Optimization Problems Based on Proximal Gradient Algorithm
item.description: arXiv:2306.11286v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper investigates a category of constrained fractional optimization problems that emerge in various practical applications. The objective function for this category is characterized by the ratio of a numerator and denominator, both being convex, semi-algebraic and differentiable with Lipschitz continuous gradients over the constraint sets. The constrained sets associated with these problems are closed, convex, and semi-algebraic. We propose an efficient algorithm that is inspired by the proximal gradient method, and we provide a thorough convergence analysis. Our algorithm is shown to converge to a critical point without the typical need for a nonnegative numerator, and this critical point becomes a globally optimal solution whenever the numerator is nonpositive at the initial point. Our approach is adaptable to unbounded constraint sets as well. Therefore, our approach is viable for many more practical models. Numerical experiments show that our method not only reliably reaches ground-truth solutions in some model problems but also outperforms several existing methods in maximizing the Sharpe ratio with real-world financial data.
item.dc:creator: Yizun Lin, Jian-Feng Cai, Zhao-Rong Lai, Cheng Li

item.title: Analysis of Primal-Dual Langevin Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2405.18098v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We analyze a recently proposed class of algorithms for the problem of sampling from probability distributions $\mu^\ast$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with a Lebesgue density of the form $\mu^\ast(x) \propto \exp(-f(Kx)-g(x))$, where $K$ is a linear operator and $f,g$ convex and non-smooth. The method is a generalization of the primal-dual hybrid gradient optimization algorithm to a sampling scheme. We give the iteration's continuous time limit, a stochastic differential equation in the joint primal-dual variable, and its mean field limit Fokker-Planck equation. Under mild conditions, the scheme converges to a unique stationary state in continuous and discrete time. Contrary to purely primal overdamped Langevin diffusion, the stationary state in continuous time does not have $\mu^\ast$ as its primal marginal. Thus, further analysis is carried out to bound the bias induced by the partial dualization, and potentially correct for it in the diffusion. Time discretizations of the diffusion lead to implementable algorithms, but, as is typical in Langevin Monte Carlo methods, introduce further bias. We prove bounds for these discretization errors, which allow to give convergence results relating the produced samples to the target. We demonstrate our findings numerically first on small-scale examples in which we can exactly verify the theoretical results, and subsequently on typical examples of larger scale from Bayesian imaging inverse problems.
item.dc:creator: Martin Burger, Matthias J. Ehrhardt, Lorenz Kuger, Lukas Weigand

item.title: Variational Analysis of Proximal Compositions and Integral Proximal Mixtures
item.description: arXiv:2408.07235v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper establishes various variational properties of parametrized versions of two convexity-preserving constructs that were recently introduced in the literature: the proximal composition of a function and a linear operator, and the integral proximal mixture of arbitrary families of functions and linear operators. We study in particular convexity, Legendre conjugacy, differentiability, Moreau envelopes, coercivity, minimizers, recession functions, and perspective functions of these constructs, as well as their asymptotic behavior as the parameter varies. The special case of the proximal expectation of a family of functions is also discussed.
item.dc:creator: Patrick L. Combettes, Diego J. Cornejo

item.title: Convergence Analysis of Stochastic Accelerated Gradient Methods for Generalized Smooth Optimizations
item.description: arXiv:2502.11125v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the Randomized Stochastic Accelerated Gradient (RSAG) method, utilizing either constant or adaptive step sizes, for stochastic optimization problems with generalized smooth objective functions. Under relaxed affine variance assumptions for the stochastic gradient noise, we establish high-probability convergence rates of order $\tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/T}\right)$ for function value gaps in the convex setting, and for the squared gradient norms in the non-convex setting. Furthermore, when the noise parameters are sufficiently small, the convergence rate improves to $\tilde{O}\left(\log(1/\delta)/T\right)$, where $T$ denotes the total number of iterations and $\delta$ is the probability margin. Our analysis is also applicable to SGD with both constant and adaptive step sizes.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Journal of Optimization Theory and Applications (2026)211:27
item.dc:creator: Chenhao Yu, Yusu Hong, Junhong Lin

item.title: A Smoothing Accelerated Proximal Gradient Method with Nonmonotone Backtracking Strategy for Convex Nonsmooth Composite Multiobjective Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2503.12915v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies convex nonsmooth composite multiobjective optimization problems, whose objectives combine a convex term admitting a smooth approximation with a proper, closed, and convex term. A natural way is to smooth the nonsmooth term and apply proximal gradient method, but reducing the smoothing parameter shrinks step sizes, and solving successive smooth approximations to approach the original solution is computationally expensive. To address this issues, we propose a smoothing accelerated proximal gradient method with nonmonotone backtracking strategy. Each outer iteration starts from a reduced base smoothness estimate, which is increased only if the criterion fails, while the momentum update is linked to the estimate through an exact identity used in the convergence analysis. Under a compact level-set assumption and bounds of parameters, we use merit function to establish rates of $\mathcal{O}(k^{-\sigma})$, $\mathcal{O}((\log k)/k)$, and $\mathcal{O}(k^{\sigma-2})$ for different smoothing parameters. Then quasi-Fej\'er monotonicity yields convergence of the full sequence to a weak Pareto solution. Numerical experiments show that the method can reduce computational cost while preserving high-quality Pareto fronts and examine how the smoothing parameter affects performance.
item.dc:creator: Huang Chengzhi

item.title: Mathematical programs with complementarity constraints and application to hyperparameter tuning
item.description: arXiv:2504.13006v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider the Mathematical Program with Complementarity Constraints (MPCC). One of the main challenges in solving this problem is the systematic failure of standard constraint qualifications. Carefully accounting for the combinatorial nature of the complementarity constraints, tractable versions of the Mangasarian-Fromovitz Constraint Qualification (MFCQ) have been designed and widely studied in the literature. This paper looks closely at two such MPCC-MFCQs and their influence on MPCC algorithms. As a key contribution, we introduce a third MPCC-MFCQ, lying between these two, under which we prove the convergence of the inexact sequential penalisation and Scholtes relaxation algorithms. This significantly weakens the assumptions currently used in the literature. We then form the problem of tuning hyperparameters of a nonlinear Support Vector Machine (SVM), a fundamental machine learning problem for classification, as an MPCC. For this application, we establish that the aforementioned new qualification holds under very mild restrictions. Moreover, we program robust implementations and carry out comprehensive numerical experiments on real-world data sets, where we show that the sequential penalisation method applied to the MPCC formulation for tuning SVM hyperparameters can outperform both the Scholtes relaxation technique and the derivative-free methods from the machine learning literature.
item.dc:creator: Samuel J. Ward, Alain Zemkoho, Selin Damla Ahipasaoglu

item.title: Successive Convexification for Passively-Safe Spacecraft Rendezvous on Near Rectilinear Halo Orbit
item.description: arXiv:2505.17251v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present an optimization-based approach for fuel-efficient spacecraft rendezvous to Gateway, a lunar space station architecture based on a near rectilinear halo orbit (NRHO) around the Earth-Moon L2 point. Our main contribution is a method that ensures safety at all times in the presence of Gaussian uncertainty while incorporating disturbance compensation feedback through correction maneuvers. Specifically, the approach: i) ensures passive safety and satisfies path constraints at all times, ii) satisfies the specifications for critical decision points along the trajectory, and iii) accounts for common uncertainties arising from orbital insertion maneuvers, actuation, and navigation measurements. To account for these uncertainties, we use both chance constraints and disturbance compensation feedback to bound the effects of errors. We leverage sequential convex programming (SCP) together with an isoperimetric reformulation of continuous-time path constraints, including passive safety, to eliminate the risk of inter-sample constraint violations common in existing methods. This enables sparse time discretization that supports efficient offline mission design and analysis and aligns with operational preferences for less frequent control actions. We demonstrate the method on a case study representative of Gateway rendezvous operations.
item.dc:creator: Purnanand Elango, Abraham P. Vinod, Kenji Kitamura, Beh\c{c}et A\c{c}{\i}kme\c{s}e, Stefano Di Cairano, Avishai Weiss

item.title: Multi-cut stochastic approximation methods for solving stochastic convex composite optimization
item.description: arXiv:2505.17463v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper considers the stochastic convex composite optimization problem and presents multi-cut stochastic approximation (SA) methods for solving it, whose models in expectation overestimate its objective function. The multi-cut model obtained by taking the maximum of a finite number of linearizations of the stochastic objective function provides a biased estimate of the objective function, with the error being uncontrollable. Instead, our proposed SA method uses models obtained by taking the maximum of a finite number of one-cut models, i.e., suitable convex combinations of linearizations of the stochastic objective function. It is shown that the proposed methods achieve nearly optimal convergence rate and have computational performance comparable, and sometimes superior, to other SA-type methods.
item.dc:creator: Jiaming Liang, Renato D. C. Monteiro, Honghao Zhang

item.title: A global stochastic maximum principle for delayed forward-backward stochastic control systems
item.description: arXiv:2601.14138v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we study a delayed forward-backward stochastic control system in which all the coefficients depend on the state and control terms, and the control domain is an arbitrary nonempty set. To handle the terms involving $y$ and $z$ in the second-order expansion, we derive two decompositions of $\big(\hat{y}^\e(\cd), \hat{z}^\e(\cd)\big)$. More precisely, we use the second decomposition to handle the terms involving $f^\e_{yy}, f^\e_{yz}$ and use both decompositions to handle the term involving $f^\e_{zz}$. Finally, a global stochastic maximum principle is obtained.
item.dc:creator: Feng Li

item.title: Almost Sure Convergence of Stochastic Approximation: An Interplay of Noise and Step Size
item.description: arXiv:2602.10580v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the almost sure convergence of the Stochastic Approximation algorithm to the fixed point $x^\star$ of a nonlinear operator under a negative drift condition and a general noise sequence with finite $p$-th moment for some $p > 1$. Classical almost sure convergence results of Stochastic Approximation are mostly analyzed for the square-integrable noise setting, and it is shown that any non-summable but square-summable step size sequence is sufficient to obtain almost sure convergence. However, such a limitation prevents wider algorithmic application. In particular, many applications in Machine Learning and Operations Research admit heavy-tailed noise with infinite variance, rendering such guarantees inapplicable. On the other hand, when a stronger condition on the noise is available, such guarantees on the step size would be too conservative, as practitioners would like to pick a larger step size for a more preferable convergence behavior. To this end, we show that any non-summable but $p$-th power summable step size sequence is sufficient to guarantee almost sure convergence, covering the gap in the literature. For the regime $p \in (1, 2)$, we show that using the $\|x-x^\star\|^p$-like Lyapunov function and applying the Holder-smoothness bound suffice. For $p > 2$, such an approach is no longer applicable, and therefore, we introduce a novel iterate projection technique to control the nonlinear terms produced by high-moment bounds and multiplicative noise. We believe our proof techniques and their implications could be of independent interest and pave the way for finite-time analysis of Stochastic Approximation under a general drift condition. As a starting point, we establish almost sure convergence results for non-expansive operators under a multiplicative noise condition for $p \in (1,2]$ and an additive noise condition for $p \in (2,\infty)$.
item.dc:creator: Hoang Huy Nguyen, Quang Dinh Thien Nguyen, Duc Anh Nguyen, Siva Theja Maguluri

item.title: Surrogate-based categorical neighborhoods for mixed-variable blackbox optimization
item.description: arXiv:2603.27839v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In simulation-based engineering, design choices are often obtained following the optimization of complex blackbox models. These models frequently involve mixed-variable domains with quantitative and categorical variables. Unlike quantitative variables, categorical variables lack an inherent structure, which makes them difficult to handle, especially in the presence of constraints. This work proposes a systematic approach to structure and model categorical variables in constrained mixed-variable blackbox optimization. Surrogate models of the objective and constraint functions are used to induce problem-specific categorical pseudo-distances. From these pseudo-distances, surrogate-based neighborhoods are constructed using notions of dominance from bi-objective optimization, jointly accounting for information from both the objective and the constraint functions. This study addresses the lack of automatic and constraint-aware categorical neighborhood construction in mixed-variable blackbox optimization. As a proof of concept, these neighborhoods are employed within CatMADS, an extension of the MADS algorithm for categorical variables. The surrogate models are Gaussian processes, and the resulting method is called CatMADS-GP. The method is benchmarked on the Cat-Suite collection of 60 mixed-variable optimization problems and compared with two external mixed-variable solvers. Data profiles indicate that CatMADS-GP achieves the best performance on this collection of problems.
item.dc:creator: Charles Audet, Youssef Diouane, Edward Hall\'e-Hannan, S\'ebastien Le Digabel, Christophe Tribes

item.title: Optimal control for a class of linear evolution equations with transformed proper orthogonal decomposition
item.description: arXiv:2603.28442v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Solving optimal control problems for high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs) is computationally expensive. As a workaround, reduced-order models (ROMs) are often employed, which replace the full PDE system and alleviate the computational burden while solving optimal control problems. However, when the underlying PDE exhibits transport-dominated behavior, standard reduced-order modeling techniques like proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) that rely on linear approximation spaces may require a large number of modes due to the slowly decaying Kolmogorov $n$-width. To overcome this challenge, we focus on the use of transformed POD as a reduced-order model, which is particularly effective in capturing low-dimensional representations of high-fidelity transport-dominated phenomena. In this work, a reduced-order model is constructed first, followed by the optimization of the reduced system. For linear systems generated by strongly continuous groups, we prove existence and uniqueness of solutions for the ROM under an explicit smallness condition on the control, as well as the existence of an optimal control for sufficiently large regularization. The numerical experiments concern the 1D linear advection equation with a subset of the general transformation groups called the shift transformations. Additionally, we compare the computational performance of the shifted POD (sPOD) method against the standard POD.
item.dc:creator: Tobias Breiten, Shubhaditya Burela, Philipp Schulze

item.title: A Continuous-Time Actor-Critic Framework for Jump-Diffusion Controls with Normalizing Flows
item.description: arXiv:2604.05398v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Continuous-time stochastic control with time-inhomogeneous jump-diffusion dynamics is central in finance and economics, but computing optimal policies is difficult under explicit time dependence, discontinuous shocks, and high dimensionality. We propose an actor-critic framework that serves as a mesh-free solver for entropy-regularized control problems and stochastic games with jumps. The approach is built on a time-inhomogeneous little q-function and an appropriate occupation measure, yielding a policy-gradient representation that accommodates time-dependent drift, volatility, and jump terms. To represent expressive stochastic policies in continuous-action spaces, we parameterize the actor using conditional normalizing flows, enabling flexible non-Gaussian policies while retaining exact likelihood evaluation for entropy regularization and policy optimization. We validate the method on time-inhomogeneous linear-quadratic control, Merton portfolio optimization, and a multi-agent portfolio game, using explicit solutions or high-accuracy benchmarks. Numerical results demonstrate stable learning under jump discontinuities, accurate approximation of optimal stochastic policies, and favorable scaling with respect to dimension and number of agents.
item.dc:creator: Liya Guo, Ruimeng Hu, Xu Yang, Yi Zhu

item.title: Consensus-based optimization with $\alpha$-stable jump processes
item.description: arXiv:2604.05626v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we introduce a CBO method that incorporates jumps driven by an $\alpha$-stable stochastic process within a kinetic framework. This approach naturally induces nonlocal stochastic effects, enhancing the exploration capabilities of the method. We formulate the dynamics at the particle level, providing a detailed description of the associated stochastic system and its asymptotic behavior. In particular, by means of a Fourier-based representation, we derive the corresponding fractional Fokker-Planck equation, which captures the nonlocal diffusion mechanisms generated by $\alpha$-stable processes. As a central result, we establish a rigorous convergence analysis for the proposed method. Finally, we assess its performance through a series of numerical experiments, highlighting the effectiveness of $\alpha$-stable jump dynamics and their advantages over standard diffusion based strategies, especially in complex optimization landscapes.
item.dc:creator: Pedro Aceves-Sanchez, Giacomo Albi, Federica Ferrarese, Michael Herty

item.title: Gradient Descent's Last Iterate is Often (slightly) Suboptimal
item.description: arXiv:2604.13870v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider the well-studied setting of minimizing a convex Lipschitz function using either gradient descent (GD) or its stochastic variant (SGD), and examine the last iterate convergence. We prove that $\Theta(\sqrt{\log(T)/T})$ is the optimal anytime rate attainable with a fixed stepsize schedule (that does not depend on the total number of steps $T$). The upper bound holds already for SGD, and improves on the $\log(T)/\sqrt{T}$ rate of Shamir and Zhang [2013], as well as the $\sqrt{\log(T)/T}$ rate of Zamani and Glineur [2023] which was proven only for deterministic GD. The matching lower bound holds already for GD, and confirms the conjecture of Jain et al. [2019], namely that the optimal $1/\sqrt{T}$ rate for the last iterate cannot be obtained without prior knowledge of $T$.
item.dc:creator: Guy Kornowski, Ohad Shamir

item.title: Generalization of Zeroth-Order Method for Quotients of Quadratic Functions
item.description: arXiv:2604.26913v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Optimization of quadratic functions and their quotients is relevant in subspace and iterative optimization methods. In this paper, we consider the matrix-free computation of the generalized operator norm and the maximization of a generalized Rayleigh quotient when only forward evaluations of two linear operators $A$ and $B$ are available. The proposed method samples search directions uniformly from the full unit sphere, thereby avoiding tangent-space sampling and explicit access to the metric matrix $B^{\mathrm T}B$. The exact line search along each sampled direction reduces to a $2\times2$ generalized eigenvalue problem on specific Gram matrices. In the generic case its maximizing step has a closed form. We prove that the objective values converge almost surely to the largest generalized eigenvalue and that the distance of the iterates to the leading generalized eigenspace converges to zero. We also relate full-sphere moment estimators to the Riemannian gradient and Hessian. The numerical experiments on synthetic Gau{\ss}ian operators illustrate the behavior of the methods, and further studies of the proposed algorithms indicate favorable empirical convergence and weak dependence on the tested problem dimensions.
item.dc:creator: Jonas Bresch

item.title: Cross-validated feature selection using least-squares support vector machines for binary classification
item.description: arXiv:2605.07089v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Support vector machines (SVMs) are widely used for binary classification. However, irrelevant or redundant features can degrade classification accuracy and model interpretability, making feature selection important for SVMs. Most SVM feature selection methods rely on sequential search or regularization and do not directly identify the best feature subset. Mixed-integer optimization (MIO) is a direct approach to best subset selection. Cross-validation (CV) is broadly applicable to feature selection because it evaluates predictive performance on validation data without model assumptions. Although Purcaru et al. (2026) proposed an MIO formulation for CV-based linear-SVM feature selection (SVM-CV), this method suffers from high computational cost. We develop computationally efficient CV-based MIO formulations for feature selection in linear SVM classification by using least squares support vector machines (LS-SVMs). We formulate the problem as a bilevel MIO problem, where the lower-level problem trains LS-SVM classifiers and the upper-level problem selects features based on validation sets. We then reformulate it as a single-level MIO problem by exploiting the optimality conditions of LS-SVM. We propose two formulations: a hinge-loss-based validation model and a least-squares-based validation model. We compare our methods with SVM-CV and other SVM-based and logistic-regression-based methods through simulation experiments on synthetic data. The hinge-loss-based validation model attained high feature selection accuracy under the high-noise and moderate-noise conditions, particularly with more candidate features, and the least-squares-based validation model performed well in feature selection under the low-noise condition at the lower correlation level. Furthermore, our two models achieved substantially faster computation than the existing SVM-CV model.
item.dc:creator: Masaharu Mori, Shunnosuke Ikeda, Ryuta Tamura, Yuichi Takano, Ryuhei Miyashiro

item.title: Proximal Limited-Memory Quasi-Newton Methods for Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2605.11627v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a regularized proximal quasi-Newton method (RPQN) for minimizing the sum of a continuously differentiable, possibly nonconvex function and a proper, lower semicontinuous, prox-bounded, possibly nonconvex regularizer. The method uses adaptive quadratic regularization and limited-memory quasi-Newton models. We establish global convergence under weak assumptions, without requiring global Lipschitz continuity of the gradient, and prove convergence of the entire sequence, with rates, under the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property. To solve the proximal subproblems efficiently, we exploit compact limited-memory representations and derive a compact representation of the Kleinmichel rank-one update, which preserves positive definiteness under the same condition as BFGS. Numerical experiments on logistic and Student's regression demonstrate competitive performance and the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
item.dc:creator: Simeon vom Dahl, Alberto De Marchi, Christian Kanzow

item.title: Convergence Analysis via ODE Approach for Convex Optimization with Linear Equality Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2605.17819v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies the continuous-time dynamics of primal-dual algorithms for linearly constrained convex optimization problems and provides a quantitative convergence analysis using the Lyapunov functions. With the growing prevalence of sparse and low-rank models, large-scale problems involving nonsmooth objective functions have become increasingly important. Our approach addresses nonsmooth and nonstrong convex objective functions, which is particularly effective in extending classical accelerated methods to broader large-scale optimization problems. Building upon the ordinary differential equation (ODE) approach inspired by the recent work on Nesterov's acceleration methods, we extend the analysis to an ODE associated with an optimization problem with linear equality constraints. Furthermore, to relax strong assumptions, we introduce two geometric conditions the Flatness condition and the Growth condition and derive explicit convergence rates depending on the local geometry and algorithmic parameter. When the objective function is convex and the Lagrangian satisfies the Flatness condition, an appropriate parameter choice yields a worst-case convergence rate of O(1/t^2). Furthermore, incorporating the Growth condition guarantees this worst-case rate of O(1/t^2) for any function satisfying these assumptions if and only if the parameter is chosen above a suitable threshold; under this condition, even faster convergence can be achieved. For the algorithmic construction, a numerical scheme is derived by discretizing the proposed ODE. We also investigate the influence of algorithm parameters and provide insights into their optimal selection. Finally, preliminary numerical experiments are provided to validate the consistency with the theoretical results.
item.dc:creator: Chise Ishii, Yasushi Narushima

item.title: Local-to-Global Exactness of SDP Relaxations for Sparse QCQPs
item.description: arXiv:2606.21823v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study exact semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxation for a given sparse quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP). The SDP relaxation is exact if, whenever it has an optimal solution, it admits a rank-at-most-one optimal solution that corresponds to an optimal solution of the QCQP. Using the maximal cliques of a chordal extension of the aggregate sparsity pattern graph of the data matrices, we formulate the SDP relaxation in terms of clique-wise matrix variables and develop a local-to-global framework for certifying exactness. For each clique-wise matrix variable, we introduce a local sub-SDP with two parameters: a local right-hand-side vector and a consistency matrix specifying the values of entries shared by overlapping clique-wise matrix variables. In the main theorem, these parameters are determined by an optimal solution of the global clique-wise SDP. The theorem shows that if the resulting local sub-SDPs are exact, then the original SDP relaxation is exact. Under the additional assumption that any two distinct cliques intersect in at most one node, we present three classes of local QCQPs that can be incorporated into this framework: convex local QCQPs, local QCQPs characterized by sign-pattern conditions, and separable local QCQPs with a limited number of constraints. Examples illustrate how these different local QCQP classes can be combined in sparse QCQPs.
item.dc:creator: Masakazu Kojima, Sunyoung Kim, Naohiko Arima

item.title: Emission-aware operation of residential PV-battery systems: the role of information structure
item.description: arXiv:2606.26648v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Residential batteries can reduce the carbon emissions of households with photovoltaic (PV) generation, but how much depends on how they are operated under uncertain load, PV generation, and grid carbon intensity. We cast the operation of a residential PV-battery system as a sequential decision problem and compare, under a common and explicit evaluation protocol, a family of linear policies that differ in the information available at decision time, in how they anticipate the future, and in their adaptivity: a rule-based self-consumption policy, an open-loop stochastic schedule, affine feedback policies, receding-horizon policies with deterministic, scenario-based and two-stage lookahead models, and perfect-information benchmarks. Scenarios are generated by a joint principal component model of the three uncertain quantities, which supports conditional sampling during the day. Experiments on Italian data at 15-minute resolution comprise single-day evaluations on 10000 test scenarios in three seasons and a closed-loop simulation over more than eight months of real data. When the state of charge is treated consistently across policies, the self-consumption rule is within 3.2% of the perfect-foresight emissions in closed loop, whereas open-loop schedules and receding-horizon policies that decide before measuring the current period are about 20--35% above it. With real-time measurements, scenario-based receding-horizon control consistently outperforms its deterministic counterpart and, for households that rely more on the grid, reduces emissions by about 5% with respect to the rule. The benefit of emission-aware optimization is therefore determined mainly by the information structure of the controller and by the size of the system relative to the demand.
item.dc:creator: Anna Sacilotto, Ambrogio Maria Bernardelli, Stefano Gualandi

item.title: Asynchronous Sensitivity-Based Distributed NMPC
item.description: arXiv:2607.03412v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper presents a cooperative distributed model predictive control (MPC) scheme for nonlinear continuous-time systems. The centralized optimal control problem is solved asynchronously via a fixed number of sensitivity-based distributed programming (SBDP) iterations. The proposed scheme requires only neighbor-to-neighbor communication and no synchronization between agents during optimization. Under nominal MPC stability and bounded information delay, local exponential stability is established for a sufficiently large number of per-agent SBDP iterations. Numerical and hardware-in-the-loop results on both Ethernet and Wi-Fi demonstrate the benefits of an asynchronous execution, reducing execution times by over 60% while maintaining comparable closed loop performance.
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Pierer von Esch, Andres V\"olz, Knut Graichen

item.title: Polyhedral Outer Approximation for MISOCP: Geometry and Progressive Integrality
item.description: arXiv:2608.10055v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Polyhedral outer approximation (OA) is widely used to solve mixed-integer second-order cone programs (MISOCPs) by iteratively strengthening polyhedral relaxations of conic constraints. However, the accumulation of cutting planes can increase the difficulty of solving the resulting mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs), while repeatedly solving these MILPs can be computationally expensive. To address these challenges, we investigate the geometry of supporting cuts and the computational role of integrality in OA. First, we establish theoretical bounds showing that the marginal contribution of a new supporting cut decreases at least linearly as its supporting direction approaches an existing one. Motivated by this analysis, we develop a closed-form cut-generation strategy that balances separation depth and directional diversity. Second, we propose a progressive-integrality OA framework that strengthens the polyhedral approximation through linear programs and partially integral relaxations before solving full MILPs. We theoretically characterize the transfer of cut-induced bound improvements across integrality levels and provide a branch-and-bound interpretation of the framework. Computational experiments on CBLIB instances and large-scale AC unit-commitment models demonstrate substantial improvements over classical OA and direct MISOCP solution, with runtime reductions of up to 62\% relative to classical OA on the reported power-system instances.
item.dc:creator: Yongzheng Dai

item.title: Mirror descent algorithms with logarithmic barriers
item.description: arXiv:2608.22834v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We derive convergence guarantees for mirror descent and proximal mirror descent with a logarithmic barrier as the distance-generating function. When the solution lies on the boundary, the Bregman divergence blows up and classical guarantees become vacuous. While existing remedies recover $O(\log k/k)$ rates by adapting classical bounds, we propose a more direct route in which the Bregman distance to the solution never appears, and which achieves the same rate with constant stepsize. We also construct an example showing that this rate cannot be improved in general. Finally, we compare the proposed approach with interior-point methods.
item.dc:creator: Alberto De Marchi, Yura Malitsky, Adrien B. Taylor

item.title: On the invariance of risk-sensitive LQR gain under input randomization
item.description: arXiv:2609.02363v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper shows that the optimal gain of the risk-sensitive linear quadratic regulator (LQR) problem is invariant under input randomization when the cost penalizes the realized noisy input. This may appear counterintuitive at first glance because certainty equivalence does not hold for risk-sensitive LQR and input randomization inflates the effective process noise. Nonetheless, the gain is preserved because the input noise enters not only the system dynamics but also the cost functional, and its total effect eventually vanishes. Consequently, the optimal gain and the Riccati recursion need not be recomputed, and the increment in the optimal cost can be readily evaluated in closed form. This result facilitates the use of risk-sensitive LQR in applications that employ input randomization for privacy or exploration, such as dynamic watermarking for replay attack detection.
item.dc:creator: Yeongjun Jang

item.title: Proximal-Linearized NEP Method for Composite Optimization with Set-Inclusion and Manifold Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2609.14564v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper focuses on difference-of-convex (DC) composite optimization problems with set-inclusion and manifold constraints. We develop an inexact proximal-linearized nonsmooth exact penalty (NEP) method that penalizes the conic constraint while retaining the manifold constraint explicitly. At each outer iteration, the method approximately solves a strongly convex proximal-linearized subproblem over the current tangent space, using computable inexactness criteria, adaptive parameters, and a retraction-based acceptance mechanism. Under boundedness of the iterates and penalty parameters, we establish an $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ worst-case outer iteration complexity for finding an $\epsilon$-approximate KKT point of the original problem. We further develop a complexity-transfer framework relating uniform primal objective-gap and KKT-residual decay, or dual objective-gap decay, to total inner-iteration complexity bounds. This yields an $O(\epsilon^{-4})$ overall oracle complexity with either accelerated semi-proximal ADMM or FISTA applied to the dual subproblem as the inner solver. Using semi-proximal ADMM as the inner solver improves the bound to $O(\epsilon^{-2}\log(1/\epsilon))$ under an additional uniform error-bound condition. We further establish convergence of the entire iterate sequence to a KKT point under the same boundedness assumption and the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property of the associated potential function. Numerical experiments demonstrate the competitive performance of the proposed method on row-sparse PCA, clustering, robust SVMs, and nonconvex SOCPs.
item.dc:creator: Hao He, Ruyu Liu, Shaohua Pan

item.title: Two Answers on Heavy-Ball Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.09912v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We determine the worst-case behavior of the heavy-ball method on smooth strongly convex functions, first for Polyak's quadratic-optimal parameters and then for arbitrary constant parameters. For Polyak's tuning, the exact dimension-uniform exponential rate is the largest growth factor of an interpolable mixture of rotating geometric sequences. Four algebraic families determine this rate at every condition number. Two frequencies suffice, and one function in dimension five attains the rate at every horizon up to constant factors. We recover the sharp convergence threshold $9+4\sqrt5$ of Badithela and Seiler. For general tunings, an exact linear feasibility criterion characterizes dimension-uniform linear convergence through the angle between the characteristic polynomials of the two extreme quadratics. This gives a continuous condition-number threshold and resolves the second heavy-ball riddle of Goujaud, Taylor and Dieuleveut. The regions between consecutive cycle tongues are Farey gaps, each containing convergent and divergent tunings. Regular portions of the threshold surface are analytic plateaus with fixed periodic frequency support. Every rational rotation number in a gap anchors a single-harmonic plateau; mixed-harmonic plateaus and an exact two-lag threshold point also occur. Along tongue edges, explicit multiplier inequalities and second-order expansions of competing Farey fans bound the transition from single-harmonic to mixed-harmonic extremals. The rate bounds and the extremal constructions follow from a common interpolation and separation argument that preserves initialization with zero momentum.
item.dc:creator: Dmitry Pasechnyuk-Vilensky, Martin Tak\'a\v{c}

item.title: 0/1 integer programming over polytopes of Chv\'atal rank one is as hard as lattice problems
item.description: arXiv:2610.10911v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A rational polyhedron has Chv\'atal rank at most one if a single round of Chv\'atal-Gomory cuts yields its integer hull. In 1973, Chv\'atal asked whether 0/1 integer programs over polytopes of bounded Chv\'atal rank can be solved in polynomial time. For polyhedra of bounded Chv\'atal rank, integer feasibility is in NP $\cap$ coNP, so it is unlikely to be NP-hard. We answer Chv\'atal's question negatively already in its most restricted form: for Chv\'atal rank one, for integer feasibility, and even for the SAT polytopes of formulas whose clauses have at most three literals. Our answer holds under either of two standard assumptions from lattice-based cryptography. First, a polynomial-time algorithm for integer feasibility on such SAT polytopes of Chv\'atal rank one would solve bounded distance decoding with polynomial factors in deterministic polynomial time, contradicting the conjectured hardness of approximating lattice problems within polynomial factors. Second, assuming the hardness of learning with errors, an average-case analog of bounded distance decoding, the problem is also hard on average, for a polynomial-time samplable distribution of formulas. This also gives negative answers to related questions of Cornu\'ejols, Lee, and Li. We first prove these results for parallelepipeds, where they rest on an elementary sufficient condition: a polyhedron has Chv\'atal rank at most one if its width is less than one along every row of some unimodular matrix. For our parallelepipeds, such a matrix exists but is hard to find. For SAT polytopes, we represent candidate lattice vectors by their residues modulo small integers, and binary arithmetic on additional 0/1 variables checks that these vectors lie in the lattice.
item.dc:creator: Alberto Del Pia

item.title: First-order Optimization Methods with Generalized Smoothness for Low-rank Matrix Factorization
item.description: arXiv:2610.19059v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies several first-order methods for low-rank matrix minimization in the Burer--Monteiro form, where the target matrix is represented as the product of a nonnegative factor matrix and its transpose. Such a factorization destroys convexity of the objective function and global Lipschitz continuity of the gradient. We prove that for a quadratic objective function that is strongly convex only on the subspace of symmetric matrices, the Burer-Monteiro factorized objective possesses generalized smoothness with a fractional exponent 2/3. For a quadratic objective, the generalized smoothness property requires positive definiteness of the operator A only on the subspace of symmetric matrices, which relaxes the assumptions of Dragomir et al. On this basis, three methods are proposed: an adaptive gradient descent method with Armijo backtracking; an unconstrained SafeAdam method combining the Adam direction with a descent-angle certificate and a fallback to the normalized gradient; and a certified projected version for the nonnegativity constraint. Global convergence and explicit convergence rates for the proposed methods have been proved. The obtained convergence rate is better than the convergence rate of ordinary unaccelerated gradient descent in the case of a sufficiently large gradient. In the small-gradient regime, the convergence guarantee is of square-root type, and the corresponding complexity scales as the inverse square of the desired accuracy. In the large-gradient regime, the convergence guarantee is of three-quarters type, and the corresponding complexity is proportional to the inverse of the accuracy raised to the power of 4/3. Experiments on SymNMF using the TDT2, Reuters and CBCL datasets, which are standard benchmarks for document and image clustering, show that the methods match or outperform Dyn-NoLips without tuning the relative-smoothness kernel parameters.
item.dc:creator: A. V. Bidanets, F. S. Stonyakin

item.title: Effective Dual Subgradient Methods Through Sequential Subgradient-Aligned Rays
item.description: arXiv:2610.31486v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we propose an efficient subgradient-based framework, referred to as the sequential subgradient-aligned rays (SSAR) method, for improving the convergence performance of the dual subgradient method. In particular, the proposed method identifies and exploits a finite sequence of rays, when available, as the dual subgradient method evolves, along each of which a subgradient of the negative dual function remains constant and aligns with the ray. While the dual variable iterates remain on each identified ray, a constant stepsize associated with the ray is employed, with the associated constant stepsizes decreasing from one ray to the next. This approach yields constant decrements in the negative dual function values while the dual variable iterates remain on the associated rays, enabling the dual variable iterates to progress more quickly toward a dual optimal solution. We then show that the proposed SSAR method can be leveraged to improve the performance of the dual decomposition method for minimizing the average of local loss functions associated with multiple agents that share a common decision variable, a widely used problem formulation in many large-scale real-world applications. In particular, the SSAR method improves the convergence performance of the corresponding dual decomposition method while also reducing its communication cost. Numerical experiments on a least squares regression problem and a logistic regression problem using real datasets are conducted to evaluate the performance of the SSAR method.
item.dc:creator: Hansi Abeynanda, Chathuranga Weeraddana, Carlo Fischione

item.title: The monopolist's free boundary problem in the plane
item.description: arXiv:2412.15505v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the Monopolist's problem with a focus on the free boundary separating bunched from unbunched consumers, especially in the plane, and give a description of $C^{1,1}(\overline{\Omega})$ solutions for the family of square domains $\{(a,a+1)^2\}_{a \ge 0}$. The Monopolist's problem is fundamental in economics, yet widely considered analytically intractable when both consumers and products have more than one degree of heterogeneity. Mathematically, the problem is to minimize a smooth, uniformly convex Lagrangian over the space of nonnegative convex functions. What results is a free boundary problem between the regions of strict and nonstrict convexity. We study both the structure of the free boundary problem on convex domains in $\mathbf{R}^n$ showing that each bunch extends to this boundary and providing a proof in $\mathbf{R}^2$ that the interior free boundary can only fail to be smooth in one of four specific ways (cusp, high frequency oscillations, stray bunch, nontransversal bunch); in addition we offer a description of $C^{1,1}(\overline{\Omega})$ solutions to Rochet and Chon\'e's example on the family of squares $\Omega = (a,a+1)^2$, where we discover bifurcations first to targeted and then to blunt bunching as the distance $a \ge 0$ to the origin is increased. To do this, we extend the localization for measures in convex-order to accommodate potential discontinuities in the product allocation map at the fixed boundary. We also employ techniques from the study of the Monge--Amp\`ere equation and the obstacle problem.
item.dc:creator: Robert J. McCann, Cale Rankin, Kelvin Shuangjian Zhang

item.title: On the Theory of Bias Tuning in Event Cameras
item.description: arXiv:2501.18788v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper lays the foundation of a theory for bias tuning in neuromorphic cameras, a novel sensing technology also known as "event cameras". We begin by formulating the high-level effect of the sensitivity biases on the camera's event rate in mathematical terms. We then show that, as a corollary of the Poincare-Miranda theorem, the commonly used tuning principles of rate budgeting and polarity balancing lead to a unique configuration of the sensitivity biases. As a corollary, we show how by adopting these principles, the multi-variable bias-tuning problem reduces to a two-parameter problem that can be resolved experimentally.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Ben-Ezra, D.E.C., Brisk, D. and Tal, A., 2026. On the theory of bias tuning in event cameras. Optics & Laser Technology, 204, p.116681
item.dc:creator: David El-Chai Ben-Ezra, Daniel Brisk, Adar Tal

item.title: Optimal regret for dynamic matching with static priorities
item.description: arXiv:2503.09762v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study centralized two-way dynamic matching markets in which agents arrive stochastically over time and wait in queues associated with their types. We focus on static priority policies that assign each agent type a fixed ranking over its neighbors and make online matching decisions using only queue availability. We propose the General Priority ($\mathbf{GP}$) policy, which builds on the Tree Priority ($\mathbf{TP}$) policy introduced in [KAG25]. Under the general position gap condition, $\mathbf{GP}$ selects matches using a nondegenerate optimal basic solution of the fluid relaxation. It prioritizes children over parents within trees and consistently gives clockwise neighbors priority over counterclockwise neighbors on each cycle. We establish the optimal all-time regret scaling $O(\epsilon^{-1})$ for $\mathbf{GP}$ on general two-way matching networks, where the general position gap $\epsilon$ measures the fluid relaxation's distance from degeneracy. In particular, this resolves the conjecture by [KAG25] on the optimal $\epsilon$-dependence for $\mathbf{TP}$.
item.dc:creator: S\"uleyman Kerimov, Pengyu Qian, Mingwei Yang, Sophie H. Yu

item.title: Regularized Unbalanced Optimal Transport with Pearson Marginal Penalties
item.description: arXiv:2503.15105v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study quadratically regularized unbalanced optimal transport with Pearson marginal penalties and a lower bound $\delta\ge0$ on the plan, including the sparse case $\delta=0$. We organize the analysis around the active interface, where the plan switches from its lower bound to larger values. We prove a Newton remainder estimate that depends linearly on the marginal measure of the boundary layer around this interface, and a maximum-norm inverse estimate uniform over all Newton derivatives and cell volumes. Together they give local superlinear convergence of semismooth Newton iteration in function space, of q-order at least $1+\alpha$ when the boundary-layer measure is $O(t^\alpha)$, and a common convergence neighborhood along each refinement sequence whose data converge uniformly. Transverse interfaces give second-order supercloseness of the discrete potentials to the cell averages of the continuum potentials. A directional curvature condition on the input data verifies the interface condition before the solution is known and yields an explicit Newton convergence radius on all sufficiently fine meshes, uniformly in the lower bound. A globalized inexact semismooth Newton iteration has mesh-independent numbers of outer iterations and of full-array operations, that is, passes over the plan array. Its output satisfies an a posteriori error bound relative to the continuum optimal plan. Experiments test the rates at transverse interfaces and at interfaces with tangencies, the curvature criterion, and the algorithmic work. All estimates hold for a fixed regularization parameter and a fixed lower bound on the densities.
item.dc:creator: Minh-Nhat Phung, Minh-Binh Tran

item.title: Position: Adopt Constraints Over Fixed Penalties in Deep Learning
item.description: arXiv:2505.20628v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deep learning models are increasingly subject to explicit requirements, or constraints, such as safety levels, fairness limits, and sparsity budgets. In practice, such requirements are often handled through fixed weighted-sum penalization: the constraints are added to the task loss with fixed coefficients, and the resulting scalarized objective is minimized. This position paper argues that fixed penalization is often ill-suited to deep learning problems with non-negotiable requirements, for three main reasons. First, in non-convex settings, the penalized and constrained problems are not, in general, equivalent, so a minimizer of the penalized objective need not solve the constrained problem. Second, a penalty coefficient sets an objective-constraint trade-off rather than the constraint level, so finding an acceptable coefficient often takes trial and error, each trial a full training run. Third, fixed penalization weakens hard requirements into soft penalties to be traded off against task performance. As a result, compliance is no longer built into the problem, and requirements can be quietly relaxed. We therefore argue that, when a deep learning problem specifies non-negotiable requirements, one should solve the constrained problem itself instead of a surrogate defined by fixed penalization.
item.dc:creator: Juan Ramirez, Meraj Hashemizadeh, Simon Lacoste-Julien

item.title: Online Learning in Stabilized Linear Dynamical Games with Adversarial Disturbances
item.description: arXiv:2506.18814v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study online learning in linear dynamical games where multiple strategic agents act on a shared state evolving according to a linear dynamical system subject to adversarial disturbances. This setting lies beyond both single-agent nonstochastic online control and classical linear-quadratic games, which typically focus on quadratic objectives and noiseless or stochastic dynamics. Each agent seeks to minimize its own sequence of convex losses under full-state observability. Following the stabilizing-baseline paradigm in nonstochastic online control, we assume access to linear controllers that stabilize the noiseless system and focus on online adaptation by learning disturbance-action corrections. This extends adversarial online control to strategic multi-agent shared-state systems, where each agent's actions shape the state trajectory and hence the realized losses of all learners. Under state-only and aggregate-input feedback models, we analyze agents running online gradient descent with memory to update their own disturbance-action policies. We prove per-agent regret bounds that are sublinear and near-optimal in the time horizon, with population dependence that varies under the specified feedback, opponent policy, and stability assumptions. In the common-interest case, where all agents have identical cost functions, we show that the induced online problem forms a time-varying potential game and derive equilibrium tracking guarantees. Together, our results provide a theoretical framework for adversarial online learning in stabilized linear dynamical games, connecting online control with learning in games.
item.dc:creator: Anas Barakat, John Lazarsfeld, Georgios Piliouras, Antonios Varvitsiotis

item.title: Wasserstein-Cram\'er-Rao Theory of Unbiased Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2511.07414v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The quantity of interest in the classical Cram\'er-Rao theory of unbiased estimation (e.g., the Cram\'er-Rao lower bound, its exact attainment for exponential families, and asymptotic efficiency of maximum likelihood estimation) is the variance, which represents the instability of an estimator when its value is compared to the value for an independently-sampled data set from the same distribution. In this paper we are interested in a quantity which represents the instability of an estimator when its value is compared to the value for an infinitesimal additive perturbation of the original data set; we refer to this as the "sensitivity" of an estimator.
